title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XXXIV
paragraphs:
“1_st Gent_. Such men as this are feathers, chips, and straws,
Carry no weight, no force.

2_d Gent_. But levity
Is causal too, and makes the sum of weight.
For power finds its place in lack of power;
Advance is cession, and the driven ship
May run aground because the helmsman’s thought
Lacked force to balance opposites.”

Peter Featherstone was buried one May morning. May in the unromantic neighborhood of Middlemarch did not always mean warmth and sunshine. That morning a cold wind swept blossoms out of the neighboring gardens and across the grassy mounds of Lowick churchyard. Racing clouds occasionally let through a shaft of light, gilding whatever happened to stand beneath it, beautiful or ugly alike. There was an unusually varied collection of objects in the churchyard, where a small crowd of country people had gathered to watch the funeral. Word had spread that it would be a “big burying.” The old gentleman had left detailed written instructions: he intended to outdo his social superiors in the splendor of his funeral. And so he had. Old Featherstone was no Harpagon, whose other passions had been swallowed by the eternally starved appetite for saving money, and who would have negotiated with his undertaker in advance. He loved money, but he also enjoyed spending it to satisfy his particular tastes. Perhaps what he enjoyed most was its power to make other people uncomfortably aware of his influence. Anyone who insists that old Featherstone must have had some good qualities will find no contradiction from me. Still, goodness is modest and easily discouraged. When shameless vices push it aside early in life, it tends to withdraw into such deep seclusion that people constructing a selfish old gentleman in theory find it easier to believe in than those whose more limited judgments come from knowing him. At any rate, he had set his heart on a grand funeral, attended by invited guests who would have preferred to stay home. He had even specified that his female relatives should follow him to the grave. Poor sister Martha had therefore made a troublesome journey from the Chalky Flats. She and Jane would have found tearful comfort in this proof that a brother who disliked their company while alive had looked forward to having it once he became a testator. Unfortunately the same invitation had gone to Mrs. Vincy, making its meaning doubtful. Her lavish expenditure on fine crape suggested the most presumptuous expectations. Worse still, her rosy complexion advertised that she was no blood relation, but belonged to that generally objectionable category, a wife’s family.

Everyone has some imagination, since images are the offspring of desire. Poor old Featherstone, who often laughed at other people’s self-deceptions, shared their illusions nevertheless. When he wrote the program for his burial, he certainly never made himself understand that he could enjoy his part in this little drama only in anticipation. As he chuckled over the troubles his dead hand would still have the grip to cause, he inevitably imagined his own awareness inhabiting that pale, motionless body. Whatever thought he gave to a future life was thus a thought of satisfaction enjoyed inside his coffin. Old Featherstone, too, was imaginative in his way.

The three mourning coaches were duly filled as the dead man’s instructions required. Mounted pallbearers wore the finest scarves and hatbands, and even the men carrying the coffin had been furnished with substantial, expensive signs of grief. Once on foot, the black procession looked still larger in the little churchyard. The heavy faces and dark clothes trembling in the wind seemed to belong to a world strangely at odds with the drifting blossoms and the sunlight flashing on the daisies. Mr. Cadwallader met them as officiating clergyman, again at Peter Featherstone’s express request, and again for characteristic reasons. He despised curates, invariably calling them understrappers, and had determined to be buried by a clergyman with a living of his own. Mr. Casaubon would never have done. Quite apart from his unwillingness to perform such duties, Featherstone particularly disliked him as his own rector, with a claim on his land through the tithe, and as the preacher of morning sermons through which the old man, wide awake in his pew, had been obliged to sit inwardly snarling. He objected to a parson perched above his head and preaching at him. With Mr. Cadwallader things had been different. The trout stream running through Mr. Casaubon’s land also crossed Featherstone’s, so this was a parson who had needed to ask a favor instead of delivering a sermon. Besides, he belonged to the upper gentry four miles from Lowick. Distance raised him into the same lofty sphere as the county sheriff and other dignitaries vaguely understood to be necessary to the order of things. Being buried by Mr. Cadwallader would be gratifying; even his name provided an excellent opportunity for deliberate mispronunciation.

It was this honor paid to the Rector of Tipton and Freshitt that brought Mrs. Cadwallader into the party watching old Featherstone’s funeral from an upstairs window at the manor. She did not much enjoy visiting the house. But, as she put it, she liked inspecting collections of curious animals, and the funeral promised just such a collection. To make the visit thoroughly agreeable, she had persuaded Sir James and the young Lady Chettam to drive her and the Rector to Lowick.
“I’ll go wherever you like with you, Mrs. Cadwallader,” Celia had said. “Only I don’t like funerals.”

“My dear, with a clergyman in the family you have to adjust your tastes. I learned that very early. On marrying Humphrey, I resolved to enjoy sermons. I began by being extremely fond of the end. The feeling soon extended to the middle and beginning, since I couldn’t have the end without them.”
“Certainly you couldn’t,” the Dowager Lady Chettam agreed with dignified emphasis.

The window commanding the funeral belonged to the room Mr. Casaubon had used while forbidden to work. Despite warnings and prescriptions, however, he had now returned to almost all his old habits. After greeting Mrs. Cadwallader politely, he had slipped back into the library to ruminate over a learned misconception concerning Cush and Mizraim.

Without these visitors, Dorothea might also have remained shut in the library. She would then have missed old Featherstone’s funeral, a scene apparently remote from the concerns of her own life, yet one which afterward returned whenever certain tender places in her memory were touched, just as her vision of St. Peter’s in Rome had become woven into feelings of despondency. Events that transform our neighbors’ lives form only the background to our own. Yet, like some particular appearance of fields and trees, they become linked with periods in our personal history. They enter the unity of experience created by the things we feel most intensely.

This dreamlike connection between something strange and poorly understood and the deepest secrets of her experience seemed to reflect Dorothea’s loneliness—a loneliness arising from the very intensity of her nature. The country gentry of earlier times breathed a thin social atmosphere. Scattered on separate stations high up the mountain, they looked down without distinguishing much in the denser layers of life below. Dorothea felt uncomfortable with both the view and the chill of that elevation.

“I’ve seen enough,” Celia said when the procession had gone into the church. She moved just behind her husband’s elbow, where she could secretly brush his coat with her cheek. “I expect Dodo enjoys it. She likes sad things and ugly people.”

“I like learning something about the people around me,” said Dorothea, who had watched everything with a monk’s curiosity on a holiday excursion. “We seem to know nothing about our neighbors unless they live in cottages. I keep wondering how other people live, and how things affect them. I’m very grateful to Mrs. Cadwallader for coming and getting me out of the library.”

“And grateful you ought to be,” Mrs. Cadwallader replied. “Your prosperous Lowick farmers are as remarkable as buffaloes or bison. I doubt you see half of them in church. They are nothing like your uncle’s tenants, or Sir James’s. Monstrosities—farmers with no landlords! One hardly knows where to put them.”

“Most of the mourners aren’t from Lowick,” Sir James said. “I imagine they’re people expecting legacies, from farther away or from Middlemarch. Lovegood says the old man has left a considerable sum of money besides his land.”

“Just imagine! While so many younger sons can’t afford their own dinners,” said Mrs. Cadwallader. The door opened and she turned. “Ah, Mr. Brooke! I felt there was someone missing, and now I know who. You’ve come to watch this extraordinary funeral, of course?”

“No, to inquire after Casaubon—see how he’s getting along, you know. And to bring some news—a little news for you, my dear.” Mr. Brooke nodded at Dorothea as she approached him. “I peeped into the library and found Casaubon at his books. I told him it was no use. ‘This won’t do at all,’ I said. ‘You must think of your wife, Casaubon.’ He promised to join us. I didn’t give him my news. I told him he must come upstairs.”

“Look, they’re leaving the church now!” cried Mrs. Cadwallader. “Good heavens, what a wonderfully assorted company! There’s Mr. Lydgate, in his medical capacity, I suppose. But that woman is really handsome, and the fair-haired young man must be her son. Do you know who they are, Sir James?”
“I can see Vincy, the Middlemarch mayor. Presumably that’s his wife and son,” Sir James answered. He looked to Mr. Brooke for confirmation; Mr. Brooke nodded and said—
“Yes, a thoroughly respectable family. Vincy is an excellent fellow, a credit to the manufacturers. You’ve met him at my house, you know.”
“Oh yes—one of your secret committee,” Mrs. Cadwallader said mischievously.
“He goes coursing, though,” said Sir James, with a fox-hunter’s contempt.

“And helps drain the life out of those miserable handloom weavers at Tipton and Freshitt. That explains his family’s smooth skins and healthy looks,” Mrs. Cadwallader said. “Those dark, purple-faced creatures set them off admirably. Goodness, they look like a row of jugs! Look at Humphrey. In his white surplice, towering over them, he might be an ugly archangel.”
“A funeral is a solemn business all the same,” Mr. Brooke observed, “when you look at it that way, you know.”
“But I don’t look at it that way. If I wore my solemnity too frequently, it would fall to pieces. The old man’s time had come, and nobody there regrets it.”
“How dreadful,” said Dorothea. “I think this funeral is the saddest sight I’ve ever seen. It darkens the whole morning. I can’t bear the thought of anyone dying without leaving love behind.”

She meant to continue, but noticed her husband entering and taking a seat a little apart. His presence did not always change her feelings happily. She sensed that he often silently disapproved of what she said.

“Really!” Mrs. Cadwallader exclaimed. “A new face has appeared from behind that broad man, stranger than any of the others. A little round head with protruding eyes—quite froglike. Do look. Surely he belongs to a different family.”

“Let me look!” said Celia, newly curious. Standing behind Mrs. Cadwallader, she leaned forward over her head. “What a peculiar face!” Then a different surprise suddenly changed her expression. “Dodo! You never mentioned that Mr. Ladislaw had come back!”
Alarm struck Dorothea. Everyone saw her turn abruptly pale and look straight up at her uncle, while Mr. Casaubon watched her.

“He came along with me, you know. He’s my guest—staying at the Grange,” said Mr. Brooke with perfect ease. He nodded at Dorothea as though this were precisely the news she should have expected. “We’ve brought the picture on top of the carriage too. I knew you’d enjoy the surprise, Casaubon. Your very likeness—as Aquinas, you know. Exactly the right thing. And you’ll hear young Ladislaw explain it. He talks remarkably well—draws your attention to this and that—understands art and all those matters. Excellent company, you know. Whatever line you take, he can keep up with you. Just what I’ve wanted for ages.”

Mr. Casaubon gave a cold, courteous bow. He controlled his irritation only enough to remain silent. Will’s letter was as present to his mind as to Dorothea’s. He had noticed its absence from the letters set aside for him during his recovery. Privately deciding that Dorothea must have written to tell Will not to come to Lowick, he had been too proudly sensitive to bring the matter up again. Now he concluded that she had arranged for her uncle to invite Will to the Grange. Dorothea felt quite unable to explain anything at that moment.

Mrs. Cadwallader had turned her eyes from the churchyard and observed a good deal of silent communication. Finding it less clear than she would have liked, she could not help asking, “Who is this Mr. Ladislaw?”

“A young relation of Mr. Casaubon’s,” Sir James answered at once. Kindness often made him perceptive and quick in personal affairs. From Dorothea’s look toward her husband, he had guessed that something frightened her.

“A most agreeable young man. Casaubon has provided everything for him,” Mr. Brooke explained. “He’s a good return on your expenditure, Casaubon,” he continued, nodding encouragingly. “I hope he’ll stay a long time, and we’ll get somewhere with my papers. I have any number of ideas and facts, you know. I can see he’s exactly the fellow to arrange them. Remembers the appropriate quotations, _omne tulit punctum_, and so on—puts things in a particular light. I asked him some time back, Casaubon, while you were ill. Dorothea said you couldn’t receive visitors, you know, and asked me to write.”

Poor Dorothea felt that each word her uncle uttered must irritate Mr. Casaubon like a grain of sand in his eye. To explain now that she had never wanted her uncle to invite Will Ladislaw would have been utterly inappropriate. She could not begin to understand her husband’s reasons for disliking his presence, although the scene in the library had made that dislike painfully clear. But she knew it would be wrong to say anything that let other people suspect it. Mr. Casaubon himself had not fully examined his mixed motives. Like the rest of us, when irritated he looked for justification rather than self-understanding. He did, however, want to conceal his feelings. Only Dorothea could detect the changes in his face before he spoke, bowing more ceremoniously and making his voice rise and fall more than usual—
“Your hospitality is most generous, my dear sir. I must express my gratitude for your extending it to a member of my family.”
By now the funeral had finished, and people were leaving the churchyard.
“You can see him now, Mrs. Cadwallader,” Celia said. “He looks exactly like the miniature of Mr. Casaubon’s aunt in Dorothea’s boudoir. Quite good-looking.”
“A very pretty young shoot,” Mrs. Cadwallader remarked dryly. “What profession is your nephew to follow, Mr. Casaubon?”
“Excuse me: he is my cousin, not my nephew.”

“Well, he’s trying out his wings, you know,” Mr. Brooke broke in. “Exactly the kind of young man who gets ahead. I’d be pleased to give him a chance. He could be a fine secretary, for instance—like Hobbes, or Milton, or Swift. That type of fellow.”
“I see,” said Mrs. Cadwallader. “Someone to write speeches.”

“Shall I bring him in now, Casaubon?” Mr. Brooke asked. “He wouldn’t enter until I’d announced him, you know. Then we can go downstairs and inspect the picture. It’s your exact likeness: a profound, subtle thinker, forefinger resting on the page, while Saint Bonaventure, or somebody, a rather stout, rosy fellow, gazes up at the Trinity. Everything has a symbolic meaning, you know. The higher kind of art. I like it within limits, but not beyond them. Keeping up with it becomes rather a strain. You’re quite at home there, though, Casaubon. And your painter does flesh well—weight, transparency, all that. I studied those matters quite deeply once. Anyway, I’ll fetch Ladislaw.”
